title: Energy, Energy Transfer & General Energy Analysis

problems.title: Kinetic energy of a car
problems.scenario:
A **1200 kg** car travels at **25 m/s**.

Find its **kinetic energy** in kJ.
hints: Divide by 1000 to convert J → kJ.
problems.solution:
Apply the kinetic-energy formula:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mV^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1200)(25)^2 = 0.5 \times 1200 \times 625 = 375\,000\ \text{J} = 375\ \text{kJ}$$

Note it scales with the *square* of speed: doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.

problems.title: Potential energy lift
problems.scenario:
A crane raises a **50 kg** load by **8.0 m**. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the gain in **potential energy** in kJ.
hints: Convert J → kJ by dividing by 1000.
problems.solution:
$$PE = mgz = 50 \times 9.81 \times 8.0 = 3924\ \text{J} = 3.924\ \text{kJ}$$

This is the minimum work the crane must do against gravity (ignoring friction and acceleration).

problems.title: Energy from an electric heater
problems.scenario:
A **2000 W** electric heater runs for **15 minutes**.

How much **electrical energy** does it consume, in kJ?
hints: Energy = power × time. Watts × seconds = joules.
problems.solution:
Electrical work is power multiplied by the running time:

$$W_e = \dot W_e\,\Delta t = 2000\ \text{W} \times (15 \times 60)\ \text{s} = 2000 \times 900 = 1\,800\,000\ \text{J} = 1800\ \text{kJ}$$

Keep time in **seconds** so that W·s = J.

problems.title: Ideal pumping power
problems.scenario:
A pump raises water at $\dot m = 20\ \text{kg/s}$ to a reservoir **15 m** higher, with negligible change in pressure and velocity. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the **ideal (minimum) power** required, in kW.
hints: The only mechanical-energy change here is potential energy.
Result is in watts — divide by 1000 for kW.
problems.solution:
With pressure and velocity unchanged, the pump only adds potential energy to the flow:

$$\dot W = \dot m\,g\,\Delta z = 20 \times 9.81 \times 15 = 2943\ \text{W} = 2.943\ \text{kW}$$

This is the *ideal* power; a real pump needs more (see the next problem).

problems.title: Pump with efficiency
problems.scenario:
The pump from the previous problem (ideal power **2.943 kW**) has a **mechanical efficiency of 0.75**.

Find the **actual shaft power** that must be supplied, in kW.
hints: $\eta_{pump} = \dot W_{ideal}/\dot W_{shaft}$, so rearrange for the input.
problems.solution:
The pump efficiency relates the useful (ideal) power to the shaft power supplied:

$$\eta_{pump} = \frac{\dot W_{ideal}}{\dot W_{shaft}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \dot W_{shaft} = \frac{\dot W_{ideal}}{\eta_{pump}}$$

$$\dot W_{shaft} = \frac{2.943}{0.75} = 3.924\ \text{kW}$$

The extra 0.98 kW is lost to friction and other irreversibilities inside the pump.

problems.title: Available wind power
problems.scenario:
Wind at **10 m/s** blows through a turbine rotor of diameter **50 m**. Air density is $\rho = 1.2\ \text{kg/m}^3$.

Find the **total available power** in the wind passing through the rotor, in kW.
hints: The available power is the kinetic energy flux: $\dot W = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot m V^2$ with $\dot m = \rho A V$.
Combine them: $\dot W = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho A V^3$. Swept area $A = \pi D^2/4$.
problems.solution:
The kinetic energy carried by the wind per unit time uses the mass flow $\dot m = \rho A V$:

$$\dot W = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot m V^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho A V^3$$

The swept area:

$$A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi (50)^2}{4} = 1963.5\ \text{m}^2$$

Then:

$$\dot W = \tfrac{1}{2}(1.2)(1963.5)(10)^3 = 0.5 \times 1.2 \times 1963.5 \times 1000 = 1\,178\,000\ \text{W} \approx 1178\ \text{kW}$$

A real turbine can extract at most 59% of this (the Betz limit), and less in practice.

problems.title: Hydroelectric power output
problems.scenario:
Water falls **90 m** through a hydroelectric plant at $\dot m = 500\ \text{kg/s}$. The combined turbine–generator efficiency is **0.84**. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the **electric power output**, in kW.
hints: First find the ideal power from the drop: $\dot W_{ideal} = \dot m\,g\,\Delta z$.
Then multiply by the efficiency (output = η × input).
problems.solution:
The available mechanical power from the falling water is:

$$\dot W_{ideal} = \dot m\,g\,\Delta z = 500 \times 9.81 \times 90 = 441\,450\ \text{W} = 441.5\ \text{kW}$$

The turbine–generator converts a fraction of it to electricity:

$$\dot W_{elec} = \eta\,\dot W_{ideal} = 0.84 \times 441.5 = 370.8\ \text{kW}$$

problems.title: Combined motor–pump efficiency
problems.scenario:
An electric **motor** (efficiency 0.90) drives a **pump** (efficiency 0.70). The useful mechanical power delivered to the fluid is **4.0 kW**.

Find the **electrical power** drawn from the grid, in kW.
problems.solution:
Chain the two devices: electricity → motor → pump → fluid. The overall efficiency is the product:

$$\eta_{overall} = \eta_{motor}\,\eta_{pump} = 0.90 \times 0.70 = 0.63$$

The electrical input needed for 4.0 kW of useful output is:

$$\dot W_{elec} = \frac{\dot W_{useful}}{\eta_{overall}} = \frac{4.0}{0.63} = 6.35\ \text{kW}$$

Losses compound — each stage takes its cut, so the grid must supply far more than the useful 4 kW.
